## Proof

We show that **yes**, $U$ can be expressed as $\exp(A)$ for a $2\times 2$ complex matrix $A$, by constructing such an $A$ explicitly.

**Setup.** Write
$$U=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}=-I+N,\qquad N:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
A direct computation gives $N^{2}=0$, so $N$ is nilpotent of index $2$.

**Key observations.**

1. Since $N^{2}=0$, the nilpotent part has a finite, exact logarithm:
$$\log(I-N)=-N-\tfrac{N^{2}}{2}-\cdots=-N,$$
and consequently
$$\exp(-N)=I-N=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

2. Over $\mathbb{C}$ we may take a logarithm of $-1$, namely $i\pi$, giving
$$\exp(i\pi I)=e^{i\pi}I=-I.$$

3. The two matrices $i\pi I$ and $-N$ commute (the identity commutes with everything), so
$$\exp(i\pi I-N)=\exp(i\pi I)\,\exp(-N).$$

**Construction.** Set
$$A:=i\pi I-N=\begin{pmatrix}i\pi&0\\-1&i\pi\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2}(\mathbb{C}).$$
Then, using the three observations above,
$$\exp(A)=\exp(i\pi I-N)=\exp(i\pi I)\exp(-N)=(-I)(I-N)=-I+N=U.$$

**Verification of the product.**
$$(-I)(I-N)=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}=U.\quad\checkmark$$

**Conclusion.** The matrix $U$ lies in the image of the exponential map $\exp:M_{2}(\mathbb{C})\to \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{2};\mathbb{C}^{2})$; an explicit preimage is
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}i\pi&0\\-1&i\pi\end{pmatrix}.$$

(Remark: this relies essentially on working over $\mathbb{C}$, where $-1$ admits the logarithm $i\pi$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ the same matrix $U$ is *not* an exponential, since a real Jordan block of size $2$ with a negative eigenvalue cannot occur as a real exponential — negative real eigenvalues of a real exponential must have Jordan blocks of even multiplicity. The problem asks for a complex $A$, so the answer is affirmative.)
